turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Aoife, come on through and sit yourself down. The nurse has you marked in, but I'd rather hear it from yourself. What's been happening?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah doctor, I'm wrecked with the wheezing. I'm after a cold and the chest stayed with me, a whistle every time I breathe out.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): A whistle on the way out. Can you put any date at all on when the cold started?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't, honestly. Sometime around the bank holiday, maybe the week before. The days have all melted into each other.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll not pin the date, so. Is the wheeze with you all the time now?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It is, yeah. Tight across the front of the chest, and a dry cough that gets me at night. I'm not bringing up anything with it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): No phlegm at all, even in the morning?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): None. Dry as a bone.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this, or shivers?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, and I'm not shivery either. I am a bit tired, but sure who isn't in this weather.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Can you finish a sentence without stopping for a breath?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh I can talk, that's no bother. It's the stairs that catch me. Two flights and I'm puffing like I ran the length of the park.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any actual pain in the chest, or is it only that tight feeling?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. Just the tightness. Not a pain pain.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the inhalers. Which of them are you actually using?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue one, the reliever. Two puffs each time, maybe five, six times a day. If I'm out in the yard it's more, the cold air goes straight for me.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the brown one?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah now. I get the blue and the brown mixed up something shocking. I had it in my head the blue was the steroid and the brown was for attacks, so the brown yoke has been sitting in the drawer. I only ever reach for the blue.

[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's the other way round. The blue is salbutamol, your reliever, a hundred micrograms a puff. The brown is beclometasone, the preventer steroid, two puffs twice a day, every day, even when you feel grand.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Two puffs twice a day. I knew it was around that, I just wasn't doing it. My mother is on at me about tablets the whole time. She's on metformin for the sugar, and my sister swallows biotin for the hair. I nearly asked you for a vitamin on the back of that, but it's not why I came.

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): You don't need a vitamin for this. Your mother's metformin and your sister's biotin belong to them, not to you. Let me say back what I've heard, and you correct me if I wander.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire away, yeah.

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wheezy and tight across the chest after a cold you can't date, a dry cough at night, no phlegm, no fever, no chest pain. The blue salbutamol two puffs, maybe five or six times a day, and the brown one left in the drawer.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the size of it. Only the wheeze is the last four or five days. The cold was before that, and the snuffles and the sore throat are gone. It's just the chest left, and I'm a bit wrecked, like I said.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Head cold gone, chest left behind. Was there something else, or will I keep going?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Only a saga from the bank holiday, nothing to do with the chest. The M50 was a pure disgrace, an hour and a half out to my cousin's in Lucan, rain coming down in sheets. Kilkenny and Tipp were on and his dog ate the remote, so we missed the second half, and then he made tea you could stand a spoon in. The weather hasn't let up since, has it?

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): It hasn't, no. I was stuck at the Red Cow in the same rain, watching it bounce off the bonnet. We'll leave Lucan there. Have you ever been in hospital with the asthma, or had steroid tablets before?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No hospital, thank God. I did have steroid tablets the once, years ago, when I was in college. They sorted me, but I couldn't tell you the name of them. I've had the asthma since I was about seventeen, and it never really went away.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ongoing since about seventeen, and no admissions. Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I can't stand the smell of it. I walk the dog most evenings, that's my bit of exercise, unless the rain is biblical the way it is this week.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies to medicines? Penicillin, or anything else you've come across?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. Nothing has ever come up.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse read your peak flow before you came in. It was three hundred and twenty litres a minute. Your best on the card is four hundred and eighty.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Three-twenty. That's well down. I can usually blow better than that when I'm right.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is down. Sit forward there and I'll have a listen.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, go on.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's a wheeze on both sides, a bit louder on the left, and no crackles. Your oxygen was ninety-seven percent on the nurse's reading, and the pulse was ninety-four.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety-four, is that high? I was legging it in from the car park. Some lad was reversing and the rain came on again. Typical.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): A bit quick, but you'd been rushing, so I won't hang the hat on the pulse. Putting it together, this is an asthma flare after a viral cold. That's my working impression. I'm not calling it definite until we see how you settle.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. A flare. I was half hoping I was being dramatic. So what are we doing?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm adding a course of prednisolone. Forty milligrams once a day, by mouth, for five days. Take it in the morning with food.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty for five days, mornings, with food. I can do that. Do I keep going with the blue one?

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the salbutamol, two puffs when you need it. If you're still hitting it five or six times a day once the tablets are in, that's too often and I want a call. Start the brown beclometasone again tonight, two puffs twice a day. You've it at home, so that's you taking it, not a new prescription.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Brown one tonight, two and two, and the blue when I need it. I'll ring if the blue is still five or six times. And if I'm not grand?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you're no better in three days, come back and see me. If it hasn't settled by then we might arrange a chest x-ray, but I'm not booking one today.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, no x-ray unless it's needed. Will the tablets have me wired? Last time I was up half the night, only I was studying for exams, so maybe that was the exams and not the tablets at all.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): They can stir up your sleep in some people. Taking them in the morning usually keeps that down. If you get very breathless, if you can't get the words out, or if the lips go blue, that's an ambulance, not a wait until the surgery opens.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Blue lips, ambulance, I've got that. I'll pick up the prednisolone at the chemist on the way home, and I'll start the brown one tonight. Thanks a million, doctor.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sound. First prednisolone in the morning, not tonight, brown inhaler tonight as you said. Mind yourself if that rain is still sitting on the M50.

spec.situation: Teenager or adult wheezy after a cold; confuses blue and brown inhaler; uses the reliever 'maybe five, six times a day'; peak flow numbers read by the nurse. Doctor adds a steroid course.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

bad.reason: Only medicine allergies were asked; general allergies not stated absent.
Dose per puff 100 micrograms was stated by doctor, not reported by patient.

omissions.text: Salbutamol use increases when she is out in the yard because cold air triggers symptoms.

The brown beclometasone inhaler was not merely discontinued; the patient had stopped using it because she had mixed up the blue and brown inhalers and believed incorrectly that the blue was the steroid and the brown was for attacks.
Previous steroid tablets for asthma 'sorted' her when she was in college.
Prednisolone should be picked up from the chemist and started in the morning, not that night; the doctor explicitly corrected this timing.
